sections.model_projection: The model projects a near-even game with Middle Tennessee winning 27.83 to 27.34, a home margin of -0.49 points. Marshall's win probability sits at 48.95%. The projected total is 55.17 points. These figures differ sharply from the market, which has Marshall as a 14-point favorite with a 58.5-point total, a gap of 14.5 points on the spread and 3.3 points under on the total.
sections.offensive_matchup: Middle Tennessee's opponent-adjusted offensive EPA per play (a measure of how many expected points each play adds, adjusted for competition) checks in at 0.168 (76th nationally), but their raw numbers from Week 1 were considerably stronger at 0.402. The more important interaction is MTSU's pass-heavy identity — a neutral-script pass rate of 60% (10th nationally) — running into a Marshall pass defense that allowed an opponent-adjusted 0.605 EPA per passing play, the worst mark in the country at 135th. That matchup strongly favors the Blue Raiders through the air. Marshall's own passing offense grades better at 0.356 EPA per pass play (40th), but it faces an MTSU pass defense that allowed 0.379 EPA per pass play (117th), so both passing attacks have exploitable secondaries to attack.
sections.quarterback_edge: Roman Gagliano is a new starter for Middle Tennessee with just five career games of 10-plus attempts and 170 career attempts, but he carries a 7.36 career yards per attempt and zero career interceptions across those reps, producing a positive quarterback index of 0.58. Carlos Del Rio-Wilson is the more experienced returning starter for Marshall with 383 career attempts, 14 qualifying games, and a 7.23 career yards per attempt, but he has thrown 13 career interceptions and carries a negative quarterback index of -0.22. The edge leans slightly to Gagliano on efficiency metrics despite his limited experience, though the small sample on both sides warrants caution.
sections.trenches: Middle Tennessee's offensive line grades well in opponent-adjusted line yards (27th, 3.26 per rush) and allowed a very low havoc rate of 6.6% (17th), meaning opposing defenses rarely disrupted their backfield. Marshall's defensive front, however, grades poorly in sack rate (123rd in opponent-adjusted sacks generated) and its run defense line yards allowed (49th) is middling, so MTSU's ground game should find some room. On the other side, Marshall's offensive line allowed a 10.9% havoc rate (113th) in opponent-adjusted figures, meaning MTSU's defense — while not a high-havoc unit at 8.7% (94th) — could still create disruption against a porous Marshall front. The overall offensive line edge is essentially neutral, with a slight lean toward MTSU.
sections.explosive_play_edge: This is the clearest edge in the game and it strongly favors Middle Tennessee. MTSU's opponent-adjusted explosive play rate (plays gaining 10-plus rushing or 20-plus passing yards) is 15.3% (13th nationally), while Marshall's defense allowed an explosive play rate of 15.0% (128th), creating a direct mismatch. Marshall's offense generated zero explosive plays in Week 1 (131st raw) and grades at just 10.3% in opponent-adjusted figures (112th), while MTSU's defense allowed 11.4% (62nd). The Blue Raiders have a significant advantage in creating chunk plays while limiting them defensively.
sections.third_down_red_zone: Middle Tennessee converts third downs at a 39.6% clip (85th) in opponent-adjusted metrics, but they face a Marshall defense that allows conversions at a 43.1% rate (111th), meaning MTSU should sustain drives. Marshall's own third-down offense is a major liability at 28.6% (128th opponent-adjusted), and MTSU's defense holds opponents to 36.8% (59th), compounding the Herd's difficulty extending possessions. In the red zone, MTSU scores touchdowns on 69% of trips (75th) against a Marshall defense that allows touchdowns on 71% of red-zone visits (96th); Marshall's red-zone offense converts at just 50.2% (130th), the second-worst mark in the country on an opponent-adjusted basis.
sections.roster_talent: Neither program carries blue-chip recruiting talent, with both teams at a 0.0 four-year blue-chip ratio. Marshall holds a modest roster continuity advantage with a continuity index of 0.63 versus MTSU's 0.38, and Marshall returns 51% of total production including 94% of passing production, giving the Thundering Herd a familiarity edge in their system. MTSU returns just 29% of total production (28% passing, 24% rushing), which is among the lower continuity figures in the sport and introduces meaningful uncertainty about how their new contributors will perform. Talent percentiles are close — MTSU at the 19th percentile, Marshall at the 13th — so neither team has a meaningful recruiting edge.
sections.recent_form: Both teams have played exactly one game, so recent form is based on a single-game sample with no multi-game trend to evaluate. In that game, MTSU scored 38 points and allowed 14 in raw terms, while Marshall was shut out 0-45, a historically poor performance. The model applies a form-shift of 0.0 for both teams, reflecting that one game is insufficient to establish a reliable trend. The raw results are noted but the opponent-adjusted blend metrics, which account for the quality of those opponents, are the primary inputs to the projection.
sections.market_movement: The spread opened at Marshall -17.5 and has moved 3.5 points toward Middle Tennessee, landing at -14.0 on DraftKings. That movement crosses the key number of 17, which amplifies its significance beyond the raw half-point count. The total moved from 57.5 to 58.5, a one-point increase. The model's projected margin of -0.49 (essentially a pick) sits 14.5 points away from the current market spread of -14.0, the largest single divergence in the package. Public betting percentages are unavailable, so the cause of the line movement cannot be attributed to any specific betting group.

sections.expected_game_script: Middle Tennessee will likely try to push pace through the air early, exploiting a Marshall secondary that allowed the worst opponent-adjusted passing EPA in the country. Gagliano's pass-first approach — MTSU ran a neutral-script pass rate of 60%, 10th nationally — should generate chunk plays against a defense that allowed explosive plays on 15% of opponent snaps. Marshall will need to lean on their passing game as well, given a run offense that graded at -0.031 EPA per rush (127th opponent-adjusted), but their own pass defense struggles create a two-way vulnerability. If MTSU converts their red-zone trips at their 69% rate against a Marshall defense allowing 71%, the Blue Raiders can build a lead that forces Marshall into obvious passing situations where their offense has historically struggled. Marshall's path to covering a large spread likely requires turnovers — they had a -2.0 turnover margin in Week 1 — and their defense generating havoc against a relatively inexperienced MTSU offense. The model sees this as a near-coin-flip game, a dramatic departure from the market's 14-point line, driven primarily by MTSU's explosive play and passing advantages overwhelming Marshall's home-field edge.
